_readme: P1 capability network (decided 2026-10-02; docs/handoff/2026-10-02/03_TECHNOLOGY_CAPABILITY_LADDER.md). Hidden from normal play; the Knowledge and Civilization views surface only what is relevant. Each node is the NEXT step beyond what Rome already does well: 'baseline' says what Rome had, 'bottleneck' what stops the next step, 'leap' how the inventor moves it (formalize, improve, combine, scale, standardize, apply) - never 'invent' what Rome had. Levels: theory, demonstrated, prototype, reproducible, manufacturable, economical, adopted, institutionalized. Rule (PROPOSED P1-07): a capability can't pass a level its prerequisites haven't reached, up to reproducible. 'carriers' are institutions whose members carry a reproducible capability forward during an absence (PROPOSED P1-09); 'echo' gives what the inventor finds on arrival at each level, and 'distorted' when bad copies spread it. P1 powered workshops (2026-10-04) added replaceable bearing blocks, controlled transmission and powered boring and grinding, the nodes the Powered Workshops challenge needs. Nodes are added only when content needs them.

capabilities.name: shared measures
capabilities.baseline: Every trade measures well by its own foot and its own rule; the state keeps standard measures for the market.
capabilities.bottleneck: Two workshops' feet differ by a finger's width, so a part made in one won't fit in the other.

echo.Reproducible: In a few shops on the Clivus and at Ostia the rules on the walls are copies of one bronze bar. The men there say a thing is cut to the foot and mean that one.
echo.Manufacturable: A founder by the river casts bronze rules from the one master and sells them stamped. Every new shop on the river buys one before it buys an anvil.
echo.Economical: Rules cut to the shared foot are cheap now, cheaper than arguing over measures. Builders' contracts on the Aventine name the foot by the founder's stamp.
echo.Adopted: Every fitter on the river works to one foot now, and the guild keeps the bronze master in its hall.
echo.Institutionalized: The guild at Ostia keeps the master foot in a locked case and checks its members' rules against it every year. A short rule costs a fine.

capabilities.name: gauges and fits
capabilities.baseline: Skilled men fit each part by hand to the part beside it.
capabilities.bottleneck: Parts made apart, by different hands, don't fit without filing.

echo.Reproducible: Three shops still cut seats to a shared set of gauges, and their pumps trade parts.
echo.Manufacturable: One shop at Ostia makes nothing but gauges, hardened plugs in pairs, and sells them to fitters up and down the river.
echo.Economical: A fitter's gauges cost less than a bad job. Shops that don't use them can't sell to the shippers, and say so bitterly.
echo.Adopted: Fitters on the quays carry fit and no-fit plugs in a leather roll, and buy seats from whichever shop is nearest.
echo.Institutionalized: The guild sells sealed sets of gauges to its members. A seat cut to them fits any member's pump, from Ostia to the Aventine.

capabilities.name: true valve seats
capabilities.baseline: Bronze force pumps with leather flaps, the kind the fire watch carries (Ctesibius's design, two centuries old).
capabilities.bottleneck: Seats wear oval and are refitted by eye, so pumps leak back on every stroke.

echo.Reproducible: In a few cellars under the Aventine the pumps still have seats cut true, refitted by men who learned it in Cassianus's cellar. Nowhere else.
echo.Manufacturable: A bronze shop on the Clivus casts seats by the dozen from one pattern and sells them in straw, ready to fit. A fitter buys three and keeps two for the next job.
echo.Economical: A true seat costs less now than a day's bailing. Bakers and fullers who never owned a pump have one in the yard, and the porters who used to bail have other work or none.
echo.Adopted: The pumps on the Ostia quays have seats cut to a gauge now. The guild's fitters carry the gauges in a box, and a pump that leaks back is a joke.
echo.Institutionalized: The guild at Ostia stamps the pumps its members fit: a seal on the casing says the seats were cut to the guild's gauge. A shipper won't buy a pump without it.
echo.distorted: You see the other kind, too: seats cut by eye to look like the good ones, leaking back on every stroke. The men who sell them say the design is the foreigner's.
echo.distorted.later: The cheap seats are still sold at the market gates, and still leak. People call them Pollio's seats now, and say the good ones were stolen from him by a foreigner.

capabilities.name: recorded trials
capabilities.baseline: Craft trial and error, and physicians' case histories in the Hippocratic tradition.
capabilities.bottleneck: Results live in one man's head and die with him.

capabilities.name: dimensioned drawings
capabilities.baseline: Architects draw plans and elevations; Vitruvius wrote down how machines are built.
capabilities.bottleneck: Drawings show the shape but not the sizes another shop would need.

capabilities.name: recipes for bronze
capabilities.baseline: Founders make fine bronzes and brass by long practice.
capabilities.bottleneck: The mix is judged by eye and tradition, so no two pours are the same.

capabilities.name: graded tool steel
capabilities.baseline: Smiths make good steel from Noric iron and harden and temper it by colour and feel.
capabilities.bottleneck: Hardness varies from batch to batch and nobody writes down why.

capabilities.name: rigid lathe work
capabilities.baseline: Bow and pole lathes turn wood, bone and soft metal.
capabilities.bottleneck: Hand power and a cutter held by hand can't hold a size in hard metal.

capabilities.name: line shafts
capabilities.baseline: Water wheels grind grain, some in great flights like the mills at Barbegal; gears are well known.

echo.Reproducible: A few shops by the river run more than one machine from a single wheel, on shafts the millwrights can take apart and put back.
echo.Manufacturable: A millwright's yard at the foot of the Janiculum sells shafts, bearing blocks and rope pulleys made to a pattern. Buyers bring the drawing; the yard brings the parts.
echo.Economical: Powered shops along the race undersell the hand shops on the Clivus. The hand shops that are left do the fine work, or close.
echo.Adopted: Every new shop on the river is built around a shaft. Men speak of a shop's 'wheel' the way they speak of a ship's hull.
echo.Institutionalized: The guild keeps a register of who may draw water for a shaft, and inspectors who look at the bearings before the wheel may turn.

capabilities.name: replaceable bearing blocks
capabilities.baseline: Mills turn on bronze and hardwood bearings, greased by hand; millwrights know their work well.
capabilities.bottleneck: A worn bearing is fitted in place, so it stops the mill for days, and no two are alike.

echo.Reproducible: Millwrights on the hill carry spare bearing shells cut to one size and change a worn one between dawn and the first grinding.
echo.Economical: Bearing shells are sold by the basket at Ostia, cheap enough that nobody waits for a worn one to fail.

capabilities.name: controlled transmission
capabilities.baseline: Gears and pinions at mills; rope drives on cranes and treadwheels.
capabilities.bottleneck: Everything on a shaft runs or stops together, and a machine can't be taken off the wheel without stopping the wheel.

echo.Reproducible: In the powered shops a boy works a lever that lets a rope go slack, and one machine stops while the others run on.

capabilities.name: powered boring and grinding
capabilities.baseline: Hand boring with bow drills and augers; grinding with abrasives and treadle wheels.
capabilities.bottleneck: A hand can't hold a bore true down a long cylinder, or grind a hundred parts alike.

echo.Reproducible: In a shed by the race a bar turns all day, boring cylinders that the men test with a plug and stack in rows.
echo.Economical: Finishing shops buy rough parts bored and ground by water and do only the last polish by hand. There are fewer finishers than there were, and they are better paid.

capabilities.name: interchangeable parts
capabilities.baseline: Bricks, tiles and lead water pipes come in standard sizes.
capabilities.bottleneck: Metal parts are still fitted one by one.

capabilities.name: the hydraulic press
capabilities.baseline: Screw presses for oil and wine; force pumps that lift water.
capabilities.bottleneck: Seals and cylinders give way long before the pressure a press needs.

capabilities.name: the governor
capabilities.baseline: Hellenistic float regulators keep a water clock's flow steady.
capabilities.bottleneck: No one has made a machine that corrects its own speed.

capabilities.name: steam power
capabilities.baseline: Hero's spinning sphere and temple devices show steam can move things.
capabilities.bottleneck: Boilers, seals and true cylinders: nothing holds pressure and does work for long.

capabilities.name: comparative case records
capabilities.baseline: Physicians write case histories and argue over them.
capabilities.bottleneck: Households' cases are never put side by side and counted.

capabilities.name: electrical experiments
capabilities.baseline: Rubbed amber draws straw; lodestone draws iron. No one uses either.
capabilities.bottleneck: No drawn wire, no insulation, no steady source.

capabilities.name: copying at scale
capabilities.baseline: Scribes copy books for the trade; seals and stamps print the same mark many times.
capabilities.bottleneck: Every copy of a text is written out by hand.
